summary:
I’m sending you a picture of Christopher, your new little half-brother. The picture was taken when he was about an hour old, which was a month ago. So he looks more human now, I’m glad to relate, and he eats all the time. He’s up to nine pounds and a half. He is a very serious baby, scowling all the time, like a critic of some sort. People say he looks like me, but as near as I can make out he is looking more and more like W.C. Fields. I think he doesn’t like babies, same as Fields. Hospital and doctor expenses wiped us out financially, but I won’t go into that because 1 remember that when my own father wrote to me he told me all his troubles, and I couldn’t have cared less. What fathers should write to their children is—well, let’s see. That it’s a good world, that the evil people eventually get theirs, that humor is more valuable than a high I.Q. or money or creative abil­ ity. What I recall from my own novels is the funny parts like: 

“I saw them making love through the door.” “They made love through the door?” 

“No, I saw them through the door. They were in the bedroom.” That’s from WE CAN BUILD YOU, which I consider one of my best novels. It’s still in print. I forget if I told you this, but my experimental novel, CONFESSIONS OF A CRAP ARTIST, is finally going to see print. Your mother may remember it; I wrote it back then, so long ago.
